paragraphs.notes: B05-01 ‘there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Odysseus’ → ‘there is not one of his subjects who has not forgotten Odysseus’: logically identical (all have forgotten him). It removes the dead negative-relative ‘but’, which can read reversed. Verified that AFTER 2 ¶13 reads ‘there is not one of you who has not forgotten Odysseus, who ruled you as though he were your father’, so Homer's verbatim repeat (2.230–234 = 5.8–12) stays parallel in the edition. The double negative costs a moment's processing but is unambiguous. The adjudicator's ‘every one … has forgotten’ would be plainer but break the parallel. Conventions and quotation structure intact.

B05-02 ‘chattering sea-crows that do their business in the waters’ → ‘… whose business is in the waters’: fixes a real hazard that the candidate introduced, since for animals ‘do their business’ means excrete. It keeps Butler's noun ‘business’ and his ‘in the waters’ (D29) and matches Homer 5.66–67 (θαλάσσια ἔργα μέμηλεν). No scatological reading remains, and ‘business’ occurs once in both Butler and the AFTER. A note on the rationale only, with no effect on the text: Butler's ‘occupy their business in … waters’ is verbatim the Coverdale (Prayer Book) Psalter of Ps. 107:23 (‘and occupy their business in great waters’); the wording quoted in the reason (‘that do business in great waters’) is the KJV.

B05-03 ‘wicker hurdles’ → ‘wicker screens’: a real hidden misreading for present-day, especially American, readers, for whom ‘hurdles’ are track barriers. ‘screens’ names the woven panels by the function the sentence itself states. ‘wicker’ and ‘fenced’ keep the material and the fencing, matching Homer ῥίπεσσι οἰσυΐνῃσι … κύματος εἶλαρ (5.256–257). This is Butler's only ‘hurdles’ in the poem. No collision and no anachronism, since ‘wicker’ blocks the electronic sense of ‘screens’. B05-04 ‘making them fast with braces and sheets’ → ‘… with the ropes called braces and sheets’: a real false friend, because after Calypso's linen ‘sheets’ reads as bed linen or sheets of cloth and ‘braces’ as supports. The three-word gloss is accurate (both are running-rigging ropes; Homer 5.260 lists ὑπέρας … πόδας). It is in narration, not dialogue, and at the first and only use of these terms in the poem, which is what the Glossary's gloss rule allows (shortest useful explanation, folded in, at first use). The edition already renders Butler's nautical ‘sheets’ as ‘ropes’ at 15 ¶24. Both of Butler's terms are kept and no dividing mark is added. Butler's paragraph has no ‘rope’ or ‘called’, so there is no collision. Pre-existing in the accepted BEFORE, not counted: ‘adzed them smooth’ → ‘trimmed them smooth’ drops the tool-specific verb, though the adze is still named earlier in the paragraph.

B05-05 ‘pressing me so hard about the dead body of Achilles’ → ‘… around the dead body of Achilles’: a real misreading of the action, since ‘pressing someone about X’ now means pressuring them on a subject. Butler's ‘about’ is spatial (Homer 5.309–310 περὶ Πηλεΐωνι θανόντι). The fix is one word, and ‘so hard’ is untouched. Collision: Butler's ‘round’ (‘stirred it round’, rendered ‘stirred the sea round with it’) is a different word in a different sense (motion), neither merged nor misleading. Quotation structure intact.

defects.quote: As he spoke, a wave broke over him
defects.explanation: B05-06 (‘a sea broke over him’ → ‘a wave broke over him’). The BEFORE was already clear and faithful. ‘a sea’ (= a heavy breaking wave) is Butler's own word and still current English: it is a standard dictionary sense, living in nautical usage. The packet itself records that the reader decoded it. The only alternative reading, the sea in general breaking over him, gives the same picture of the action, so no agent, action or consequence is misread. ¶22's ‘a tremendous sea got up’ and ‘what a sea the winds are raising’ prime the sense immediately before. The remaining rationale, separating two senses Butler writes with one word, is an editorial preference and not a comprehension repair: D26 forbids merging, but it does not require splitting. Secondarily, Butler's nautical ‘a sea’ carries the magnitude of Homer's μέγα κῦμα, which the plain ‘a wave’ slightly flattens, though the force survives in ‘with such terrific fury’. The AFTER is faithful and harmless. This is a revert-optional defect, not a meaning error.
defects.proposed_fix: Revert to the BEFORE: ‘As he spoke, a sea broke over him’ (Butler's own word). If the lead rules that a landsman's reading of ‘a sea’ is a genuine barrier, ‘a wave’ is an acceptable, faithful alternative, but it should be recorded as a discretionary change, not a comprehension fix.

paragraphs.notes: B05-07 ‘both sail and yard went over’ → ‘both sail and yardarm went over’: CLEAN. It is a real problem, since ‘yard’ alone reads as a garden or three feet, and every other ‘yard’ in the edition (8 ¶3, 9 ¶10, 9 ¶13, … 23 ¶27) is an enclosure. ‘yardarm’ is Butler's own word for the same spar in ¶19 (‘yard arm’; Homer ἐπίκριον at both 5.254 and 5.318), so the repair restores Butler (D29) and links the spar Odysseus built to the one he loses. Standard closed spelling, no collision. Scope: the paragraph's only differences are B05-06 and B05-07.

B05-08 ‘Then the god stayed his stream’ → ‘Then the god stopped his stream’: transitive ‘stay’ meaning stop is a listed dead sense, and ‘stayed’ now means remained. Verified that the edition renders Butler's other instances as ‘stop’ (3 ¶26 ‘stopped them’, 4 ¶2 ‘stopped their horses’, 24 ¶42 ‘did not stop it’), and that after this edit every surviving ‘stay’ in the AFTER is intransitive (remain or keep). This was the one leftover, from treating ‘staid’ as a spelling variant. Although the reader decoded it, this applies an established edition-wide rule and is not mere rewording, unlike B05-06. It matches Homer 5.451 (παῦσεν ῥόον) and keeps Butler's st-/st- pairing with ‘stilled’. Butler's paragraph has no ‘stop’, so there is no collision.

B05-09 ‘hides a brand as fire-seed’ → ‘hides a burning brand as fire-seed’: a real problem, since the dominant current sense of ‘brand’ is a trademark, and the simile's key noun is otherwise dark until ‘ashes’. ‘burning’ makes explicit what Butler's ‘brand’ (a burning or charred piece of wood; Homer δαλός 5.488) already means and what ‘fire-seed’ requires, so it invents no detail. The edition already renders Butler's ‘firebrand’ as ‘burning brand’ at 19 ¶7. This is the only ‘brand’ in Butler, and his paragraph has no ‘burn’, so there is no collision.

The fixes to real problems (B05-02 excretion reading, B05-05 ‘pressing … about’, B05-03 ‘hurdles’, B05-04 ‘sheets’ after linen, B05-07 ‘yard’, B05-09 ‘brand’) are faithful and minimal.
